items.en: The First Dhyāna: Its Threefold World and Marks of Arising
items.zh: 通明觀 · 初禪發相 · 三種世間

zh: 次釋初禪發相，如前引經說，此應具釋五支證相。今先據覺支為本，覺義既成，釋餘四支則從可見。所以經言「覺、大覺」。覺者，覺根本禪，覺觸發相，故名為覺。此事如前說，但輕重有異。大覺者，豁然心目開明，明見三事發相，名為大覺。此傍釋，未是正意。復次，今當分別覺、大覺義。所言覺者，覺世間相也；大覺，出世間也。此即對真、俗二諦釋之，亦有漏、無漏，義意在此。
en: Next, explaining the mark of the first dhyāna's own arising, as already cited above from the sūtra: this should be explained in full, the mark of realizing all five factors. Here, the factor of initial thought is first taken as the basis — once its sense is established, the remaining four factors may then be readily seen by the same pattern.

Hence the sūtra speaks of "initial thought, great initial thought." As for "initial thought": awakening to the root dhyāna, aware of the mark of tactile sensation's own arising — this is named initial thought. This matter is as already described above, differing only in its degree, light or heavy. As for "great initial thought": the mind's own eye opening suddenly into clarity, clearly seeing the mark of these three matters' own arising — this is named great initial thought. This, however, is only a peripheral explanation, not yet the proper intent.

Furthermore, the sense of initial thought and great initial thought shall now be properly distinguished. As for what is meant by "initial thought": awakening to the mark of the mundane world. "Great initial thought" means awakening to the world-transcending. This explains them with reference to the two truths, the ultimate and the conventional, and to the contaminated and the uncontaminated — the sense intended here lies precisely in this.

zh: 今明世間則有三種：一、根本世間，一期正報五陰是也；二、義世間者，知根本之法，與外一切法義理相關也；三、事世間者，發五通時，悉見一切眾生種類及世間事也。世間既有三種，出世間對世間亦為三。所以者何？眾生根有下、中、上、利、鈍不等，是故雖同證此初禪，境界淺深，其實有異，故須約三義分別證初禪不同。第一、先釋約根本世間、出世間明覺大覺五支成初禪之相，即為二意：第一、先明初禪發相；第二、即釋成覺大覺五支差別之相。一、先明初禪發之相，即為三意，品次不同：一者、初發；二、次；三、後。
en: Here, "the mundane world" is itself clarified as being of three kinds: first, the root world, which is precisely the five aggregates of one's own present life's karmic retribution; second, the world of meaning, which means knowing that the dharma of the root world is itself interrelated, in principle, with every external dharma whatsoever; and third, the world of phenomena, which means, once the five supernormal powers are brought forth, seeing directly every kind of sentient being and every mundane matter whatsoever. Since the mundane world is thus of three kinds, the world-transcending, too, is correspondingly distinguished into three, set against the mundane. Why is this? Sentient beings' own faculties differ — lower, middle, upper, sharp, and dull, not all the same — and so, although they alike realize this same first dhyāna, the depth of their own state actually differs. Hence realizing the first dhyāna must be distinguished according to these three senses.

First, explaining, with reference to the root world and the world-transcending, how initial thought and great initial thought, together with the five factors, form the mark of the first dhyāna: this itself has two parts — first, clarifying beforehand the mark of the first dhyāna's own arising; and second, explaining how this constitutes the differentiated mark of initial thought, great initial thought, and the five factors. First, clarifying beforehand the mark of the first dhyāna's own arising: this itself has three parts, differing in grade and sequence — the initial arising; the middle; and the final.

The three-world scheme (root, meaning, phenomena) is this fascicle's own organizing structure and worth holding in mind for everything that follows: the same five factors of the first dhyāna will be explained three separate times, once through each world, because a sharp-faculty practitioner's realization genuinely reaches further than a dull-faculty practitioner's, even though both are said to attain "the same first dhyāna." What follows next — the marks of the first dhyāna's own arising — belongs to the root world, the most basic and universal of the three.

zh: 一、初發相。行者發初禪時，即豁然見自身九萬九千毛孔空疎，氣息遍身毛孔出入。雖心眼明見遍身出入，而入無積聚，出無分散，來無所經由，去無所履涉，即見身內三十六物一一分明。三十六物者：諸髮、毛、爪、齒、薄皮、厚皮、筋、肉、骨、髓、脾、腎、心、肝、肺、小腸、大腸、胃、胞、膽、屎、尿、垢、汗、淚、涕、唾、膿、血、脈、黃痰、白痰、癊、肪、𦙽、腦膜。此三十六物，十是外物，二十六是內物；二十二是地物，十四是水物。已見風、水、地相分明，復覺諸物各有熱氣煎煮，火相分明。觀此四大猶如四蛇同處一篋，四大蚖蛇，其性各異；亦如屠牛之人，分肉為四分，諦觀四分，各不相關。行者亦爾，心大驚悟。
en: First, the mark of initial arising: the practitioner, at the very moment the first dhyāna arises, suddenly sees the ninety-nine thousand pores of one's own body opening loosely, the breath's own energy going out and entering through every pore of the body. Although the mind's own eye clearly sees this going out and entering throughout the whole body, the in-breath gathers nowhere, and the out-breath scatters nowhere, coming by no particular course and going by no particular path — and one thereby sees, within the body, each of the thirty-six substances clearly and distinctly.

The thirty-six substances are: head-hair, body-hair, nails, teeth, thin skin, thick skin, sinews, flesh, bones, marrow, spleen, kidneys, heart, liver, lungs, small intestine, large intestine, stomach, bladder, gall, feces, urine, grime, sweat, tears, mucus, saliva, pus, blood, vessels, yellow phlegm, white phlegm, lymph, fat, membrane-fat, and brain-membrane. Of these thirty-six substances, ten are external, and twenty-six are internal; twenty-two belong to the earth element, and fourteen belong to the water element.

Having already seen the marks of wind, water, and earth clearly, one further perceives that each of these substances carries its own heat, simmering and boiling — the mark of fire, too, now clear and distinct. Contemplating these four elements, it is as though four snakes shared a single basket together — the four elements as four venomous serpents, each of a differing nature; or it is like a butcher dividing an ox's meat into four portions, closely observing these four portions as entirely unrelated to one another. The practitioner is exactly the same, the mind greatly startled into awakening.

zh: 復次，行者非但見身三十六物四大假合，不淨可惡，亦覺知五種不淨之相。何等為五？一者、見外十物相不淨，心生厭患，是名自相不淨；二者、見身內二十六物內性不淨，是名自性不淨；三者、自覺此身從歌羅邏時，父母精血和合以為身種，是名種子不淨；四者、此身處胎之時，在生、熟二臟之間，是名生處不淨；五者、及其此身死後，捐棄塚間，壞爛臭穢，是名究竟不淨。當知此身從始至終，不淨所成，無一可樂，甚可厭惡，我為無目，忽於昔來，著此不淨臭爛之身，造生死業於無量劫，今始覺悟，悲喜交懷。五種不淨，如《摩訶衍論》廣說。復覺定內心識，緣諸境界，念念不停，諸心數法相續而起，所念相異，亦復非一，是名初禪初證之相。
en: Furthermore: the practitioner, seeing not only that the body's thirty-six substances are the four elements only provisionally combined, impure and repugnant, also becomes aware of five distinct marks of impurity. What are these five? First, seeing the mark of the ten external substances as impure, the mind gives rise to weariness and disgust — this is named the impurity of its own mark. Second, seeing the twenty-six internal substances' own inward nature as impure — this is named the impurity of its own nature. Third, becoming aware, of oneself, that this very body, from the moment of kalala onward, is formed from the combined seed and blood of one's parents — this is named the impurity of the seed. Fourth, this body, at the time it dwells within the womb, resides between the two organs of the raw and the cooked — this is named the impurity of the place of birth. And fifth, once this body has died, it is discarded within the graveyard, decaying and rotting, foul and putrid — this is named the ultimate impurity.

One should know that this body, from beginning to end, is made up entirely of impurity, with nothing in it worth delighting in, deeply repugnant — I, having been without eyes, have heedlessly, since time immemorial, clung to this impure, rotting body, creating the karma of birth-and-death across measureless kalpas, and only now am I first awakening to this, sorrow and joy mingling together in my heart. These five kinds of impurity are given at length within the Mahāyāna treatise. One further perceives that, within this very concentration, mind and consciousness, taking various states as their object, never remain still for a single moment, the various mental factors arising in unbroken succession, the object of each thought differing from the last, not of one kind only — this is named the mark of the first dhyāna's initial realization.

The four-snakes-in-one-basket and butcher's-four-portions similes are among this treatise's most visceral images, chosen precisely because they refuse any comforting unity: the four elements composing "the body" are shown as each of a differing nature and unrelated to one another, sharing only proximity, not a genuine whole. The five kinds of impurity extend fascicle 3's earlier three-part account (from the internal expedient means) into a fuller five-part scheme spanning outward appearance, inward substance, conception, gestation, and death — the same basic content this treatise has returned to repeatedly, now anchored to an intensely detailed, first-person visionary experience rather than a doctrinal list.

zh: 次明中證相。行者住此定內，三昧漸深，覺息後五臟內生息相各異，所謂青、黃、赤、白、黑等，隨臟色別，出至毛孔。若從根入色，相亦不同。如是分別，氣相非一。復見此身薄皮、厚皮、膜、肉各有九十九重，大骨、小骨三百六十，及髓各有九十八重。於此骨肉之間有諸蟲，四頭、四口、九十九尾，如是形相非一，乃至出入、來去、音聲、言語亦悉覺知。唯腦有四分，分有十四重。身內五臟，葉葉相覆，猶如蓮華，孔竅空疎，內外相通，亦各有九十九重。諸物之間亦各有八十戶蟲，於內住止，互相使役。
en: Next, clarifying the mark of the middle realization. The practitioner, abiding within this very concentration, samādhi growing gradually deeper, perceives that, behind the breath, the five internal organs each give rise to their own differing breath-mark — namely, blue, yellow, red, white, and black, each differing according to its own organ's color, issuing out through the pores. Depending on which faculty it enters through, its color, too, differs. Distinguishing in this way, the marks of this energy are not of one kind only.

One further sees that this body's thin skin, thick skin, membranes, and flesh each have ninety-nine layers; the large and small bones number three hundred sixty; and the marrow, too, has ninety-eight layers each. Between this flesh and bone are various parasites, each with four heads, four mouths, and ninety-nine tails, their forms not of one kind only — and one becomes fully aware, further, of their own movement, coming and going, sounds, and speech as well. The brain alone has four sections, each section having fourteen layers. Within the body, the five internal organs, leaf upon leaf covering one another, are just like a lotus flower, their apertures open and porous, inward and outward freely interpenetrating, each likewise having ninety-nine layers. Between these various substances, there are also, in each case, eighty households of parasites dwelling within, each set to their own task, mutually employing one another.

zh: 若行者心靜細時，亦於定內聞諸蟲語言音聲，或時因此發解眾生言語三昧。身內諸脈，心脈為主，復從心脈內生四大之脈，一大各十脈，十脈之內一一復各九脈，合成四百脈。從頭至足，四百四脈內悉有風氣血流相注。此脈血之內亦有諸細微之蟲依脈而住。行者如是知，是知身內外不實，猶如芭蕉。復觀心數，隨所緣時，悉有受、想、行、識四心差別不同。
en: If the practitioner's mind grows still and fine, one may also hear, within this very concentration, the sound of these various parasites' own speech, and, at times, through this, come to understand the samādhi that comprehends the speech of sentient beings. Among the body's various vessels, the heart-vessel serves as the ruling one, and, from within the heart-vessel, the vessels of the four elements arise in turn, each element having ten vessels, and, within each of these ten vessels, nine further vessels each, combining to make four hundred vessels in all. From head to foot, within these four hundred and four vessels, wind, energy, and the flow of blood all pour through and irrigate one another. Within this very blood of the vessels, there are also various fine, subtle parasites dwelling, depending on the vessels for their own existence. The practitioner, knowing all this, thereby knows the body, within and without, to be unreal, just like a plantain trunk. One further contemplates the mental factors, and, whatever object is taken up, sensation, perception, formation, and consciousness, these four states of mind, are each found to differ from one another.

zh: 三、明後證之相。行者三昧智慧轉深淨明利。復見氣息調和，同為一相，如瑠璃器，非青、黃、赤、白。亦見息之出入無常生滅，悉皆空寂，復見身相新新，無常代謝。所以者何？飲食是外四大，入腹資身時，新四大既生，當知故身隨滅，譬如草木，新葉既生，故葉便落，身亦如是。愚夫不了，謂是惜身；智者於三昧內覺此身相無常所遷，新新生滅，空無自性，色不可得。復各一念心生之時，即有六十剎那生滅。或有人言：「六百剎那，生滅迅速，空無自性，心不可得。」
en: Third, clarifying the mark of the final realization. The practitioner's samādhi and wisdom grow ever deeper, purer, and sharper. One further sees the breath's own energy grown harmonious, become a single, unified mark, like a vessel of lapis lazuli, no longer distinctly blue, yellow, red, or white. One also sees the breath's own entering and leaving as impermanent, arising and ceasing, entirely empty and still, and further sees the body's own mark as ever-new, impermanent, constantly replacing itself.

Why is this? Food and drink are external instances of the four elements; entering the belly and nourishing the body, once this new instance of the four elements has arisen, one should know that the old body correspondingly perishes — just as, with grass and trees, once a new leaf has grown, the old leaf accordingly falls; the body is exactly the same. The foolish, not understanding this, cherish and cling to the body; the wise, within this very samādhi, perceive this bodily mark as shifted by impermanence, ever newly arising and ceasing, empty, without any nature of its own, its form nowhere to be found. Further still, within the arising of a single thought-moment, sixty instants of arising and ceasing are already present. Some, further, say: six hundred instants, arising and ceasing with such swiftness that it, too, is empty, without any nature of its own, the mind itself nowhere to be found.

The escalation across these three stages traces a single arc from multiplicity to unity: the initial stage sees the body's parts as radically distinct and unrelated to one another (four snakes in one basket); the middle stage multiplies this detail even further, down to parasites with four heads and ninety-nine tails, and even their audible speech; and the final stage collapses everything — the four colors, the countless layers and vessels — into "a single, unified mark, like a vessel of lapis lazuli," where impermanence itself, not the body's parts, becomes the object of contemplation. The sixty-versus-six-hundred-instants disagreement, left unresolved, is a rare case of the treatise citing a numerical dispute without adjudicating it — the exact count matters less than the shared conclusion that thought-moments are far too swift for any fixed "mind" to be found within them.

quiz.q: Why is the factor of initial thought taken as the basis in explaining the first dhyāna's arising?
options: once its sense is established, the other four may be seen likewise
quiz.why: Once the sense of initial thought is established, the remaining four factors can be readily seen by the same pattern.

quiz.q: What is the peripheral explanation of initial thought and great initial thought, and how does the text regard it?
options: initial thought is awareness of the root dhyāna's sensations; great is the mind's eye opening to see the three matters; this is peripheral, not the proper intent
quiz.why: Initial thought is awareness of the root dhyāna's arising sensations; great initial thought is the mind's eye opening to see the three matters. This is only peripheral; the proper sense follows.

quiz.q: Which description of the three kinds of world is correct?
options: the root world is this life's five aggregates; the world of meaning relates them to all external dharmas; the world of phenomena is seeing beings and affairs through the five powers
quiz.why: The root world is the five aggregates of this life; the world of meaning is their interrelation with all external dharmas; the world of phenomena is seeing beings and worldly affairs once the five powers arise.

quiz.q: Why must realizing the first dhyāna be distinguished by three kinds of world?
options: beings' faculties differ, so though they realize the same first dhyāna its depth differs
quiz.why: Faculties differ, so though all realize the first dhyāna, the depth of their state differs; the three worlds correspond to lower, middle, and upper faculties.

quiz.q: At the initial arising, what does the practitioner suddenly see?
options: the ninety-nine thousand pores open, the breath passing through them, and the thirty-six substances clearly
quiz.why: One suddenly sees the body's ninety-nine thousand pores open and the breath passing through them, and then each of the thirty-six substances clearly.

quiz.q: How are the thirty-six substances classified?
options: ten external and twenty-six internal; twenty-two earth and fourteen water
quiz.why: Ten are external and twenty-six internal; twenty-two belong to earth and fourteen to water. Fire and wind are seen through heat and breath.

quiz.q: What two similes describe the four elements?
options: four snakes sharing a basket; a butcher dividing an ox into four portions
quiz.why: The four elements are like four snakes sharing a basket, each of a different nature, and like a butcher dividing an ox into four unrelated portions.

quiz.q: Among the five impurities, what is the impurity of the seed?
options: dwelling between the raw and cooked organs
from the kalala stage, the body is formed from the parents' combined seed and blood
quiz.why: The seed impurity is that the body, from the kalala stage, is formed from the parents' seed and blood. The others are external mark, place of birth, and ultimate impurity.

quiz.q: What are the impurity of the place of birth and the ultimate impurity?
options: the womb between the raw and cooked organs; after death, rotting in the graveyard
quiz.why: In the womb the body lies between the raw and cooked organs; after death it is discarded in the graveyard to rot.

quiz.q: Having seen the body as impure from beginning to end, how does the practitioner feel?
options: reproaching oneself as eyeless for clinging to it, now awakening, sorrow and joy mingle
quiz.why: One reflects that, eyeless, one clung to this foul body for countless kalpas creating birth-and-death karma, and now awakening, sorrow and joy mingle.

quiz.q: In the final point of the first realization, what does the practitioner perceive about mind?
options: within concentration, mind takes objects without pause, mental factors arising in succession, each thought different
quiz.why: Within concentration, mind and consciousness take objects without pause, the mental factors arise in succession, and each thought differs; this is the first realization.

quiz.q: In the middle realization, what are the breath-marks arising from the five organs like?
options: different colors—blue, yellow, red, white, black—according to each organ, issuing through the pores
quiz.why: Each organ produces a breath of its own color—blue, yellow, red, white, black—issuing through the pores. Only in the final realization do they become one, like lapis lazuli.

quiz.q: Which figure about the body in the middle realization is correct?
options: three hundred sixty bones; the brain has four sections of fourteen layers each
quiz.why: There are three hundred sixty large and small bones, and the brain has four sections of fourteen layers. The organs have ninety-nine layers; eighty is the number of parasite households.

quiz.q: How does the text describe the vessels of the body?
options: the heart-vessel rules; four element-vessels of ten each, each with nine more, making four hundred
quiz.why: The heart-vessel rules; from it arise vessels for each element, ten each, and within each nine more, four hundred in all; fine parasites dwell in the blood.

quiz.q: In the final realization, what does the breath become?
options: harmonized into a single mark, like a lapis-lazuli vessel, no longer colored
quiz.why: The breath grows harmonious into one mark, like a lapis-lazuli vessel, no longer distinctly colored; one also sees its impermanence.

quiz.q: How does the text explain the body as "ever-new," arising and ceasing?
options: food is external elements; when new elements arise the old body perishes, like new leaves replacing old
quiz.why: Food is external elements; when it nourishes the body the new elements arise and the old body perishes, like a new leaf replacing an old one.
